THOUGHT: The patient is a 23-year-old previously healthy male who experienced sudden loss of consciousness (syncope) during intense physical exertion (pitching in baseball), with no trauma, no prodromal symptoms, and requiring CPR—indicating a likely life-threatening arrhythmia or hemodynamic collapse. Syncope in young athletes is a red flag for underlying cardiac pathology, especially when occurring during exertion. Key clinical clues include: (1) prominent A waves on JVP (suggesting elevated left ventricular filling pressures and impaired relaxation), (2) double apical impulse (a classic sign of hypertrophied left ventricle with forceful septal contraction and delayed posterior wall motion), (3) S4 gallop (indicative of stiff, noncompliant left ventricle with atrial contraction against high resistance), and (4) absence of murmurs—though HCM may be non-obstructive initially. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy; echocardiogram and cardiac MRI confirm asymmetric septal hypertrophy, reduced LV cavity size, and preserved systolic function—all hallmark features of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). Genetic testing confirms pathogenic mutations associated with HCM, establishing a definitive etiology. Importantly, HCM is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, often triggered by exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation) due to myocardial disarray, ischemia, and abnormal electrophysiological substrate. The absence of prior symptoms is typical, as many individuals with HCM are asymptomatic until the first catastrophic event.

DIAGNOSIS: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
